source_metadata.title: Continuous Intravenous Heparin Compared with Intermittent Subcutaneous Heparin in the Initial Treatment of Proximal-Vein Thrombosis
source_metadata.journal: The New England Journal of Medicine

atoms.canonical_statement: The trial compared continuous intravenous heparin with intermittent adjusted-dose subcutaneous heparin as initial therapy for proximal-vein thrombosis and examined whether anticoagulant intensity was related to recurrent venous thromboembolism.
Eligible patients had proximal deep-vein thrombosis involving the popliteal or a more proximal deep vein, with or without calf-vein thrombosis, demonstrated by venography.

population.label: Patients considered for trial entry
inclusion_criteria: Proximal DVT involving popliteal or more proximal veins, with or without calf-vein thrombosis

atoms.canonical_statement: Patients with active bleeding contraindicating heparin were excluded.
Patients already receiving intravenous heparin at referral were excluded.

population.label: Patients excluded because already receiving IV heparin at referral
exclusion_criteria: Already receiving intravenous heparin at referral

atoms.canonical_statement: Patients who could not be followed as outpatients because they lived too far from the hospital were excluded.

population.label: Patients excluded because outpatient follow-up was not feasible
exclusion_criteria: Unable to complete outpatient follow-up because of distance

atoms.canonical_statement: One hundred fifteen consecutive eligible patients who consented were randomized: 58 to continuous intravenous heparin and subcutaneous placebo, and 57 to subcutaneous heparin and continuous intravenous placebo.

population.label: Consecutive consenting patients with objectively demonstrated proximal deep-vein thrombosis

atoms.canonical_statement: The treatment groups were similar at entry in age distribution, sex, presentation status, history of previous deep-vein thrombosis, and listed underlying disorders.

population.label: Consecutive consenting patients with objectively demonstrated proximal deep-vein thrombosis

atoms.canonical_statement: Before randomization, patients were stratified by whether they had a history of previous venous thrombosis, and a computer-generated prescribed randomization arrangement assigned heparin treatment.

The comparison was double-blind; masked prelabeled syringes and intravenous packs were used, dose adjustments were made simultaneously in both regimens, and treating consultants adjusted doses without knowing treatment assignment.
All patients received a 5,000-USP-unit intravenous heparin bolus; the continuous-infusion group then received an initial heparin infusion equivalent to 29,760 units per 24 hours.

exposures.details: All patients received a 5,000-USP-unit IV heparin bolus; the IV arm then received heparin infused at 31 mL/hour from 20,000 units in 500 mL solution, corresponding to 29,760 units per 24 hours initially.

atoms.canonical_statement: All patients received a 5,000-USP-unit intravenous heparin bolus; the subcutaneous group then received 15,000 units subcutaneously every 12 hours (30,000 units per day initially) plus continuous intravenous placebo.

exposures.details: All patients received a 5,000-USP-unit IV heparin bolus; the subcutaneous arm then received 15,000 units every 12 hours (30,000 units/day initially) plus continuous IV placebo.

atoms.canonical_statement: Both heparin regimens were adjusted daily using a mid-interval activated partial thromboplastin time target of 55 to 75 seconds, equivalent to 1.57 to 2.14 times the mean normal control and approximately 0.20 to 0.40 heparin unit per milliliter.

outcome.definition: Target 55-75 seconds using Dade Actin-Fs reagent; approximately 1.57-2.14 times mean normal control and 0.20-0.40 heparin unit/mL

atoms.canonical_statement: Warfarin sodium was started on heparin day 6 or 7 at 10 mg per day, heparin was stopped on day 10, and warfarin was continued for 12 weeks with dose adjustment to the trial prothrombin-time range.

exposures.details: Started on heparin day 6 or 7; heparin stopped on day 10; warfarin dose adjusted during hospitalization to a prothrombin-time ratio 1.25-1.5 and continued for 12 weeks.

atoms.canonical_statement: Patients were examined daily during initial heparin therapy and followed for three months; objective testing at 3, 6, and 12 weeks included examination, impedance plethysmography, fibrinogen leg scanning, and venography when prespecified criteria were met.

Recurrent venous thrombosis required objective evidence of a new constant intraluminal filling defect on venography or conversion of previously negative leg scanning or impedance plethysmography to positive in the absence of known false-positive clinical disorders.

outcome.definition: Objective new venographic filling defect or specified conversion of objective noninvasive tests

atoms.canonical_statement: Pulmonary embolism was defined by a high-probability ventilation-perfusion lung scan, a positive pulmonary angiogram, or pulmonary embolism found at autopsy.

outcome.definition: High-probability V/Q scan, positive pulmonary angiogram, or autopsy finding

atoms.canonical_statement: Major bleeding was overt bleeding with a hemoglobin fall of at least 2 g/dL, transfusion of at least two units of blood, retroperitoneal bleeding, bleeding into a major prosthetic joint, or intracranial bleeding; other overt bleeding was minor.

outcome.definition: Overt bleeding meeting the trial hemoglobin/transfusion/anatomic criteria

atoms.canonical_statement: Fisher exact tests compared recurrent venous thromboembolism and bleeding frequencies between treatment groups; repeated-measures analysis of variance evaluated mean APTT, heparin level, and heparin dose.
Recurrent venous thromboembolism occurred in 11 of 57 patients (19.3%) assigned subcutaneous heparin versus 3 of 58 patients (5.2%) assigned continuous intravenous heparin (P=0.024).

atoms.canonical_statement: After excluding the subcutaneous-group patient whose recurrent thrombosis was attributable to inability to receive long-term warfarin because of major bleeding, recurrent venous thromboembolism remained more frequent with subcutaneous heparin: 10 of 57 (17.5%) versus 3 of 58 (5.2%) with intravenous heparin (P=0.043).

atoms.canonical_statement: A subtherapeutic anticoagulant response during the initial 24 hours or longer occurred in 36 of 57 subcutaneous-heparin patients (63.2%) versus 17 of 58 intravenous-heparin patients (29.3%) (P<0.001).

atoms.canonical_statement: Six of 57 patients (10.5%) in the subcutaneous-heparin group and 3 of 58 (5.2%) in the intravenous-heparin group died during the study (P=0.322).

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors concluded that the trial established the efficacy of continuous intravenous heparin for initial treatment of proximal venous thrombosis.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors concluded in retrospect that the tested subcutaneous heparin regimen was inadequate for initial therapy because it produced a substantially less intense early anticoagulant response.

exposures.details: All patients received a 5,000-USP-unit IV heparin bolus; the subcutaneous arm then received 15,000 units every 12 hours (30,000 units/day initially) plus continuous IV placebo.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors interpreted the data as evidence that inadequate initial anticoagulation places patients with proximal-vein thrombosis at substantial risk of recurrent venous thromboembolism.

outcome.measurement_method: Objective testing according to prespecified criteria
